course: CMU 21-254: Linear Algebra and Vector Calculus for Engineers
audience: SI leader teaching live on a whiteboard. This is not a student worksheet.
toneRule: Keep explanations very simple, verbal, and board-friendly. Avoid textbook phrasing unless the problem needs it.
title: Double Integrals, Change of Variables, and Green's Theorem
sessionGoal: Students should be able to set up double integrals, use polar coordinates when helpful, and apply Green's Theorem to convert a line integral to a double integral.
quickStartIfUnprepared: Start with the sentence: always draw the region first.
Do Problem 1 to practice switching order.
Do Problem 2 to practice polar coordinates.
Do Problem 3 to practice Green's Theorem and orientation.
sayThisFirst: For double integrals, the region matters as much as the function.
When switching order, redraw the region and rewrite the bounds.
Use polar when the region has circles, disks, or angles.
Green's Theorem changes a closed line integral into a double integral over the region inside.
boardPlan: Write 'draw first' at the top of the board.
Do one polar integral over a disk/half-disk.
Do one Green's Theorem problem over a rectangle.
keyFormulas: Green's Theorem: \(\oint_C P\,dx+Q\,dy=\iint_D(Q_x-P_y)\,dA\), for positive orientation.
For switching order: describe the same region using the other variable as the outside bound.
commonMistakes: Not drawing the region before changing bounds.
Using Green's Theorem when the curve is not closed.
Forgetting that clockwise orientation changes the sign.
notationWarnings: Use \(D\) for the region and \(C=\partial D\) for its boundary.
For Green's Theorem, clearly identify \(P\) and \(Q\).
Write 'CCW' or 'clockwise' near the boundary arrows.

problems.title: Switch order and evaluate
problems.studentPromptLatex: Rewrite the integral with the order reversed, then evaluate: \[\int_0^2\int_x^2 (x+y)\,dy\,dx.\]
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: read the bounds as inequalities, then draw the region.

visualSpec.regionDescription: Triangle bounded by y=x, y=2, and x=0.
drawInstructions: Draw the triangle bounded by x=0, y=x, and y=2.
Show vertical slices for the original order.
Show horizontal slices for the reversed order.
Label reversed bounds: \(0\le y\le 2\) and \(0\le x\le y\).

walkthrough.label: Describe the region
walkthrough.latex: The original bounds say \[0\le x\le2,\qquad x\le y\le2.\] This is the triangle above \(y=x\), below \(y=2\), and to the right of \(x=0\).

walkthrough.label: Reverse the order
walkthrough.latex: Using horizontal slices, \(y\) goes from \(0\) to \(2\). For a fixed \(y\), \(x\) goes from \(0\) to \(y\). So \[\int_0^2\int_x^2 (x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^2\int_0^y (x+y)\,dx\,dy.\]

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the lower y-value is 0 in the reversed order.
Changing the region while changing the order.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 9 for double integrals and changing order.

problems.title: Polar integral over a half disk
problems.studentPromptLatex: Evaluate \(\iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,dA\), where \(D\) is the upper half disk \(x^2+y^2\le4\), \(y\ge0\).
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: circles should make you think polar. Also, never forget the extra r in dA.

drawInstructions: Draw the upper half disk of radius 2.

walkthrough.label: Convert the region
walkthrough.latex: For the upper half disk of radius 2, \[0\le r\le2,\qquad 0\le\theta\le\pi.\]

walkthrough.label: Convert the integrand and area element

commonMistakes: Using \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\) for the upper half disk.
Leaving the integrand as \(x^2+y^2\) after switching to polar.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 9 for polar coordinates and change of variables.

problems.title: Green's Theorem over a rectangle
problems.studentPromptLatex: Let \(C\) be the positively oriented boundary of the rectangle \(0\le x\le3\), \(0\le y\le2\). Use Green's Theorem to compute \[\oint_C (x-y^2)\,dx+(2xy)\,dy.\]
problems.whatToSayBefore: Say: positively oriented means counterclockwise. Green's Theorem turns the boundary integral into an area integral.

drawInstructions: Put counterclockwise arrows on the boundary.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that positive orientation is counterclockwise.
Trying to compute the four boundary integrals directly when Green's Theorem is faster.

practiceLabPointer.note: Practice Lab Section 9 for Green's Theorem.

wrapUpQuestions: What is the first thing you should do for any double integral region?
When should polar coordinates be considered?
What are the two signs to be careful with in Green's Theorem?
qualityControlNotes: Checked Green's Theorem integrand 4y and value 24.
Visual specs include exact regions and orientation arrows.
reviewSummary: Session 21 is ready with checked double-integral, polar, and Green's Theorem problems.

open.title: Draw first
say: Today's three tools: switching the order of a double integral, polar coordinates, and Green's theorem. They look different, but every one of them starts the same way: draw the region.
If you remember one habit from today, make it this: nobody sets up a double integral without a picture.

idea.title: Slices, and the boundary that knows the inside
say: A double integral stacks up thin slices. Vertical slices mean dy on the inside; horizontal slices mean dx on the inside. Same region, same answer, just a different way of cutting it.
In polar, the slices are wedges and rings. A small polar cell has area r dr dθ: cells far from the origin are bigger, and that extra r is the thing people forget.
Green's theorem says the circulation around a closed curve equals the total spin (the 2D curl) inside it. Walk around the fence, or add up the spin in the field. Same number.
draw: Draw a triangle twice: once filled with vertical strips, once with horizontal strips.
Draw a polar grid with one small cell shaded, labeled 'width dr, arc length r dθ'.
Draw a rectangle with counterclockwise arrows on its edge and little spinning circles inside.

ask.q: Why is a polar cell's area r dr dθ and not dr dθ?
ask.a: Its arc side has length r dθ, which grows with r.

ask.q: In Green's theorem, what happens if you go clockwise?

launch.say: Reverse the order of integration, then evaluate. Draw the region before anything else.
circulate: Is there a sketch on every paper?
Watch for 'x from y to 2', the classic wrong flip.
Ask early finishers to evaluate in the original order too and compare.

steps.say: Those inequalities describe the triangle above y = x, below y = 2, right of x = 0. Corners: (0, 0), (0, 2), (2, 2).

ask.q: Where are the vertical slices in the original order?
ask.a: Each runs from the line y = x up to y = 2.

steps.say: Horizontal slices: y runs 0 to 2, and each slice goes from x = 0 across to x = y.

ask.q: Why x ≤ y and not y ≤ x?
ask.a: The region is above y = x, so on a horizontal slice x stays left of the line: x ≤ y.

steps.why: Switching order never changes the region, only how you describe it. The picture keeps you honest.

steps.say: Inner: [x²/2 + xy] from 0 to y = 3y²/2. Outer: ∫₀² 3y²/2 dy = 4.

ask.a: Area 2 times the average of x + y (at the centroid (2/3, 4/3), that's 2) gives 4. ✓

si21-p1.meaning: Same triangle, cut two ways. Adding up x + y over it gives 4 either way; the new order just makes the arithmetic cleaner.

ifStuck.if: a student writes x from y to 2
ifStuck.then: draw one horizontal slice and ask where it starts and stops.

si21-p1.transition: Rectangular slices were fine for a triangle. For a half-disk they'd be painful. Time for polar.

launch.say: Integrate x² + y² over the upper half-disk of radius 2.

askFirst.q: What in this problem says 'use polar'?
askFirst.a: The disk boundary and the x² + y² integrand.

ask.q: What would the right half-disk be?

steps.say: x² + y² = r², and dA = r dr dθ, so the integrand becomes r³.

ask.a: r² comes from the integrand and one more r from dA.

steps.why: Forget the r and you'd get 8π/3 instead of 4π.

steps.say: The r-integral gives 2⁴/4 = 4. Nothing depends on θ, so multiply by π: 4π.

ask.q: Why does θ just multiply by π?
ask.a: Nothing in the integrand depends on θ.

si21-p2.meaning: The integrand is squared distance from the origin, which is largest near the rim. Polar lets us add up rings of equal distance.

ifStuck.then: ask them to find the area of a half-disk of radius 1 with their setup. It should be π/2; without the r they get π.

si21-p2.transition: Last one: a line integral around a closed loop, turned into a double integral.

launch.say: Use Green's theorem to compute the circulation around the rectangle.

askFirst.a: Counterclockwise, with the region on your left.

steps.say: P = x − y² (with dx), Q = 2xy (with dy).

ask.q: How do you tell P from Q?
ask.a: P rides with dx, Q rides with dy.
The field's spin (2D curl) at each point.

steps.why: Green says circulation around the edge = total spin inside.

steps.say: It's a rectangle, so the bounds are just numbers: y from 0 to 2, x from 0 to 3.

ask.q: How many line integrals did we skip?

ask.a: Average of 4y over the rectangle is 4 (at y = 1), times area 6: 24. ✓

si21-p3.meaning: The field spins counterclockwise everywhere above the x-axis, more so higher up. Adding up all that spin gives the total circulation around the fence: 24.

ifStuck.then: check the order: Q_x − P_y, not P_y − Q_x.

wrap.write: Draw first. Switch order = same region, new slices. Polar: dA = r dr dθ. Green: ∮ P dx + Q dy = ∬ (Q_x − P_y) dA, counterclockwise.

exit.q: First thing for any double integral?

exit.a: Circles, disks, sectors, or x² + y² in the integrand.

exit.q: Two signs to watch in Green's theorem?
exit.a: Q_x − P_y (not the reverse), and counterclockwise orientation.
